about: Single mantras from across the Ṛgveda and beyond, one a day, from the months before Sri Hari began working through whole hymns.
Hymns to call back the mind of Subandhu, a priest who lay near death. His brothers, the seers Bandhu, Śrutabandhu and Viprabandhu, plead for his mind to return from wherever it has wandered.
The hymn of the cosmic Person, from whose sacrifice the world, the Vedas and the order of society are said to arise.
A hymn to Śrī, goddess of prosperity and radiance, kept among the supplementary (khila) hymns of the Ṛgveda.
Two hymns to Manyu, spirited resolve or righteous anger, invoked as a god who brings victory.
A hymn to Indra as the warrior without rival, recited for protection. Hence its name, the Apratiratha ‘armour’.
Speech herself speaks in the first person: “I move with the Rudras and the Vasus…”. The seer is Vāk, daughter of Ambhṛṇa.
A prayer that neither distress nor wrongdoing may reach the one whom Mitra, Varuṇa and Aryaman protect.
“May auspicious thoughts come to us from every side.” A prayer to all the gods for blessing and a full span of life.
A hymn to Night, the goddess who shines with the stars and keeps the wolf and the thief away.
Three verses to the dappled one, the Sun, moving between earth and sky.
The great riddle hymn of Dīrghatamas, with its one-wheeled chariot, its seven horses, and the line “Truth is one; the wise call it by many names”.
A hymn in praise of Agni, the fire who brings wealth, strength and renown.
Nearly every line begins śaṃ naḥ, “may it bring us peace”: a litany of well-being asked of every god and every power of nature.
Kutsa’s hymn to Agni Jātavedas, with its refrain: “O Agni, in your friendship may we come to no harm.”
The wedding of Sūryā, daughter of the Sun, to Soma: the Ṛgveda’s great marriage hymn, still recited at weddings today.
A hymn to the healing plants, spoken by the physician-seer Bhiṣag Ātharvaṇa. The plants are addressed as mothers and goddesses, born three ages before the gods.

The hymn of the Golden Embryo, seen by Hiraṇyagarbha Prājāpatya. Each verse asks “to which god shall we offer our oblation?” and answers with the one who was there before creation, upholding earth and heaven.
